title: Verb + preposition 5: in/into/with/to/on
subtitle: believe in, crash into, fill with, happen to, insist on
summary: Use in, into, with, to and on correctly after verbs such as believe, crash, provide, prefer and insist.

lesson.heading: Verb + in
lesson.text: **believe in** something = believe that it exists, or believe that it is good to do it. **specialise in** and **succeed in** also take **in**.

examples.note: = do you believe that God exists?

examples.text: I **believe in** saying what I think.
examples.note: = I believe it is right to say what I think

examples.text: Helen is a lawyer. She **specialises in** company law.
I hope you **succeed in** finding the job you want.

left.label: believe IN something
left.text: = believe that it exists / that it is a good thing
examples: I **believe in** saying what I think.

right.label: believe something / somebody (no preposition)
right.text: = believe that it is true / believe what they say
examples: The story can't be true. I don't **believe it**. (not believe in it)

lesson.heading: Verb + into
lesson.text: **break into** a house, **crash / drive / bump / run into** something, **divide / cut / split** something **into** two or more parts, and **translate** a book **from** one language **into** another.

examples.text: Our house was **broken into** a few days ago, but nothing was stolen.
He lost control of the car and **crashed into** a wall.
The book is **divided into** three parts.
She's a famous writer. Her books have been **translated into** many languages.

lesson.heading: Verb + with
lesson.text: **collide with** something, **fill** something **with** something, and **provide / supply somebody with** something. Note that the adjective is different: something is full of water, but you fill it with water.

examples.text: There was an accident this morning. A bus **collided with** a car.
Take this saucepan and **fill it with** water.
The school **provides** all its students **with** books.

lesson.heading: Verb + to
lesson.text: **happen to** somebody / something, **invite somebody to** a party or a wedding, and **prefer** one thing **to** another.

examples.text: What **happened to** that gold watch you used to have?
They only **invited** a few people **to** their wedding.

lesson.heading: Verb + on
lesson.text: **concentrate on** something, **insist on** (doing) something, and **spend** money **on** something.

examples.text: I tried to **concentrate on** my work, but I kept thinking about other things.
I wanted to go alone, but some friends of mine **insisted on** coming with me.
How much do you **spend on** food each week?

lesson.text: Movement or change goes with **into**: crash into a wall, break into a house, divide into parts, translate into English.

exercises.prompt: I haven't seen Mike for ages. I wonder what has happened ___ him.
It's a very large house. It's ___ four apartments.
exercises.explanation: divide / split / cut something INTO parts.

exercises.prompt: We've been ___ the party, but unfortunately we can't go.
exercises.explanation: invite somebody TO a party / a wedding etc.

exercises.prompt: Which preposition is missing: in, into or with?

items.text: A burglar is someone who breaks ___ a house to steal things.
Steve told me to fill the bucket ___ water.
The teacher decided to split the class ___ four groups.
The school provides all its students ___ books.
Ben was injured when he collided ___ another player.
I hope you succeed ___ getting what you want.

exercises.prompt: I don't mind big cities, but I prefer small towns. Say this in one sentence with prefer.
exercises.answer: I prefer small towns to big cities.

exercises.prompt: This morning I bought a pair of shoes, which cost eighty pounds. Say this with spend.
exercises.answer: This morning I spent eighty pounds on a pair of shoes.

exercises.statement: I was amazed when I heard the news. I couldn't believe in it.
exercises.explanation: I couldn't believe it. believe something (no preposition) = believe that it is true. believe in = believe that something exists.

exercises.prompt: Don't try and do two things together. ___ one thing at a time.
Some things are difficult to translate from one language ___ another.
exercises.explanation: translate FROM one language INTO another.

exercises.statement: I was quite cold, but Tom insisted on having the window open.

exercises.prompt: Match the beginning of each sentence with its ending.

pairs.left: Mark decided to give up sport to concentrate
My present job isn't wonderful, but I prefer it
Patrick is a photographer. He specialises
There was an awful noise as the car crashed

pairs.right: with all the information I needed.

exercises.prompt: The car in front of me stopped suddenly. Unfortunately I couldn't stop in time and ___ the back of it.
exercises.explanation: crash / drive / bump / run INTO something.
